content: PIM1, also known as proto-oncogene serine/threonine-protein kinase Pim-1, is an enzyme encoded by the PIM1 gene in humans. This gene encodes a serine/threonine kinase that plays a significant role in various cellular processes. The Pim-1 oncogene was initially identified in murine T-cell lymphomas, where it was frequently activated by the Moloney murine leukemia virus. Since then, it has been implicated in several human cancers, including prostate cancer, acute myeloid leukemia, and other hematopoietic malignancies. Pim-1 is predominantly expressed in tissues such as the spleen, thymus, bone marrow, prostate, oral epithelial cells, hippocampus, and fetal liver cells. It is also highly expressed in cell cultures derived from human tumors. Functionally, Pim-1 is involved in regulating cell cycle progression, apoptosis, transcriptional activation, and general signal transduction pathways. The PIM1 gene spans approximately 5 kilobases of DNA and contains six exons and five introns. Its expression is regulated by the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, with transcription factors STAT3 and STAT5 directly binding to the Pim-1 promoter to initiate its transcription. The PIM1 gene is evolutionarily conserved across various species, including dogs, cows, mice, rats, zebrafish, and C. elegans. Interestingly, mice deficient in Pim-1 exhibit no significant phenotypic abnormalities, suggesting functional redundancy with other kinases. Indeed, two other kinases, Pim-2 and Pim-3, share structural and functional similarities with Pim-1. The PIM1 gene produces two protein isoforms, 34 kDa and 44 kDa, due to multiple translation initiation sites. The Pim-1 protein consists of 313 amino acids and exhibits a high degree of conservation among humans, mice, and rats, with 94–97% amino acid identity. Its active site, spanning amino acids 38–290, contains conserved motifs such as a glycine loop, a phosphate-binding site, and a proton acceptor site. A single amino acid substitution at position 67 (lysine to methionine) results in the inactivation of the kinase. Pim-1 is primarily involved in cytokine signaling and participates in numerous signal transduction pathways. Its transcription is regulated by cytokines that influence the STAT pathway, including interleukins (IL-2, IL-3, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-12, IL-15), prolactin, TNFα, EGF, and IFNγ. Pim-1 can also bind to negative regulators of the JAK/STAT pathway, creating a negative feedback loop. Although the post-transcriptional modifications of Pim-1 are not well understood, it is hypothesized that Hsp90 facilitates its folding and stabilization. Additionally, the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2 has been shown to degrade Pim-1. Pim-1 interacts with various proteins, including CBX3, CDC25A, Hsp90, NFATC1, nuclear mitotic apparatus protein 1, p21, SND1, and RELA. It also binds to proteins involved in transcription regulation, such as nuclear adaptor protein p100, HP-1, PAP-1, and TRAF2/SNX6, as well as regulators of the JAK/STAT pathway, such as SOCS1 and SOCS3. Furthermore, Pim-1 acts as a cofactor for c-Myc, a transcription factor that regulates approximately 15% of all genes, and their synergy has been implicated in prostate tumorigenesis. Pim-1 is capable of phosphorylating numerous targets, including itself, many of which are involved in cell cycle regulation. Pim-1 activates proteins such as Cdc25C, a positive regulator of the G1/S and G2/M transitions, thereby promoting cell cycle progression. Conversely, it deactivates pro-apoptotic proteins like Bad, enhancing cell survival, and negative regulators of the cell cycle, such as CKI and C-TAK1, facilitating G1/S and G2/M transitions, respectively. Clinically, Pim-1 is directly involved in regulating cell cycle progression and apoptosis and has been implicated in various cancers, including prostate cancer, Burkitt’s lymphoma, oral cancer, and numerous hematopoietic lymphomas. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the PIM1 gene have been associated with an increased risk of lung cancer in Korean patients and have also been identified in diffuse large B-cell lymphomas. Beyond its role in cancer, Pim kinase inhibitors have shown potential as treatments for Alzheimer’s disease. Pim-1 expression has been linked to resistance to anti-angiogenic agents in prostate and colon cancer models, although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. A significant number of small-molecule inhibitors targeting Pim-1 have been developed. While clinical trials have demonstrated promising anti-cancer activity, issues with insufficient selectivity and associated side effects remain a challenge. Ongoing research aims to develop more potent and selective inhibitors for this target.
